questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy
questions.learningObjective: state the military office the Constitution gives the President
questions.stem: Article II vests the executive power in a President and then describes the military office that goes with it. Which statement matches the clause the text actually contains?

options.text: The President is Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States
The President is Commander in Chief of every state militia at all times and without condition
options.misconception: believes the militia limb carries no condition at all

options.text: The President commands the Army only once the Senate has concurred in a declaration of war
options.misconception: believes a declaration of war is a precondition to the command

options.text: The President's military command is a privilege the legislature may withdraw at any time by statute
options.misconception: believes the command is a revocable statutory privilege

questions.explanation: The clause reads that the President is Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy of the United States, and of the Militia of the several States. Two features of that wording matter. The command over the Army and the Navy is stated without any condition, while the militia is named only when called into the actual Service of the United States, so the states' own companies are not swept in by the President's office alone. And the command comes from the Constitution itself, not from a statute, so the legislature cannot withdraw it by a later act, though it remains the body that raises and supports the forces the President commands. The power to declare war sits in the legislature, and a declaration is therefore not what makes the command exist.
questions.hint: Look for the option that quotes the two federal forces the clause names, and drops the qualifier attached to the third.

questions.topic: The condition attached to state militias
questions.learningObjective: identify the condition the Constitution puts on the militia limb of the command clause
questions.stem: The command clause names the militia of the several States but attaches a condition to that mention. Which condition does the text state?

options.text: The militia is named whenever a state calls its own companies to active duty
options.misconception: believes a state's own call is what brings the militia within the clause

options.text: The militia is named only after a declaration of war has been enacted by both houses
options.misconception: believes a declaration of war is required before the clause reaches a militia

options.text: The militia is named while the state remains a party to a mutual defence arrangement abroad
options.misconception: believes a foreign treaty condition governs the clause

options.text: The militia is named only when it is called into the actual Service of the United States

questions.explanation: The words that follow the mention of the militia are the qualifier that keeps the clause within reach: the militia is named only when it is called into the actual Service of the United States. A state that organises companies for its own local purposes has not thereby placed them under presidential command, and no declaration of war is mentioned anywhere in the clause. The separate militia clauses supply the mechanism that produces the condition, authorising Congress to provide for calling forth the militia to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions, and to govern the part of the militia employed in the service of the United States. A call into federal service is what the President commands; a call by a state is what a state commands.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen to the militia before the President commands it, and check that the answer is in the clause itself.

questions.topic: The fraction of senators present that must concur in a treaty
questions.learningObjective: state from what base the two-thirds figure in the treaty clause is computed
questions.stem: A treaty is made by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, and the clause fixes the size of the approving group. From what base is that size measured?

options.text: A simple majority of the senators present, with the two-thirds figure reserved for impeachment
options.misconception: believes a simple majority suffices for a treaty

options.text: Two thirds of the senators present, but only after the other chamber has agreed to the same terms
options.misconception: adds a requirement of agreement by the other chamber

options.text: Two thirds of the senators present, counted from the senators actually present and not from the whole chamber
Two thirds of all the senators in the chamber, counted from the full hundred seats
options.misconception: measures the fraction against the full membership of the chamber

questions.explanation: The clause provides that two thirds of the Senators present concur. The denominator is the senators present, not the full membership of the chamber, so the number needed changes with attendance: a two-thirds fraction of ninety is sixty, while a two-thirds fraction of a full hundred is sixty-seven, and the clause asks only for the first kind of figure. The fraction is also fixed: a simple majority is not what the clause asks for. Nothing in the clause involves the other chamber, so a House vote is neither required nor contemplated. Reading the fraction against the whole chamber is the ordinary slip, and it produces a higher bar than the words demand whenever senators are absent.
questions.hint: Ask who must concur and what the words of the clause count, not what a reader might assume.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two institutions named in the treaty clause
questions.learningObjective: assign the negotiating and consenting roles in the treaty clause
questions.stem: The treaty clause divides one power between two institutions. Which description follows from the words it uses?

options.text: The President makes treaties alone, and the Senate's advice and consent is a formality recorded after signature
options.misconception: treats the consent as a formality after signature

options.text: The President makes treaties by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, two thirds of the senators present concurring
The Senate makes treaties by and with the advice and consent of the President, who consents after negotiation ends
options.misconception: reverses the two roles the clause assigns

options.text: Both chambers must concur before any negotiation may begin, so the Senate's role is only a final ratification
options.misconception: gives the other chamber a treaty role it does not have

questions.explanation: The words are that the President has power, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur. The verb is make, and the Senate is joined to it by the phrase by and with, which places the Senate inside the act of making rather than after it. The clause therefore cannot be read as giving the President a power the Senate merely advises upon afterwards, and it says nothing about the other chamber, so no concurrence of the House is part of the requirement. A president who wants a treaty has to assemble the votes inside the Senate, and that is the practical reason the two-thirds figure is fixed in the text rather than left to chamber practice.
questions.hint: Read the verbs: the clause assigns one act and one supporting step, and the question is which institution performs each.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The unsettled question after the Senate votes to concur in a treaty
questions.learningObjective: identify the disputed question that follows Senate concurrence in a treaty
questions.stem: Suppose the Senate votes by the required fraction to concur in a treaty that has been negotiated. The public disagreement over the consequences of that vote turns on a question the Constitution does not settle. Which question is that?

options.text: Whether the President's duty to carry the agreed terms into effect is a judicially enforceable duty or a political one
Whether a treaty becomes valid only when the President signs it after the Senate has concurred
options.misconception: treats a presidential signature as a condition of validity

options.text: Whether the concurrence of the other chamber is a silent precondition to a treaty's entry into force
options.misconception: believes the other chamber must concur before entry into force

options.text: Whether the fraction of senators that must concur is measured from those present or from those appointed
options.misconception: reduces the dispute to a head count of the Senate

questions.explanation: The clause tells us when the power is exercised and how many senators must concur, but it is silent on what follows if a President, having obtained the concurrence, declines to proceed. The disagreement divides over whether the resulting obligation is enforceable in court or is a political duty whose breach the courts will not examine; earlier judicial treatment of the question was narrow, and later decisions took a more open view. The other three options are not open at all. The President's signature is part of the making of a treaty rather than a condition added to a finished act, the other chamber has no treaty role under this clause, and the fraction is measured from the senators present, which the clause itself settles.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four points the clause itself answers, and discard those, then ask what remains genuinely undecided.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The documents named in the supremacy clause
questions.learningObjective: identify what the supremacy clause makes the supreme law of the land
questions.stem: One clause names the instruments that bind every state judge notwithstanding a contrary state law. Which entry does that clause make?

options.text: The Constitution, its amendments, the laws of the United States, and treaties made under United States authority
options.misconception: adds the amendments, which the clause does not name

options.text: All laws of the United States and all treaties, whether or not they were made under United States authority
options.misconception: drops the requirement that a treaty be made under United States authority

options.text: State constitutions, in addition to the laws of the United States and treaties made under United States authority
options.misconception: treats a state constitution as part of the supreme law

options.text: The Constitution, the laws of the United States made in pursuance of it, and treaties made under the authority of the United States

questions.explanation: The clause reads that this Constitution, and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, are the supreme law of the land. Two limits are written into that sentence and are often lost in summary. The laws count only if made in pursuance of the Constitution, and the treaties only if made under the authority of the United States. The amendments are not named in the clause, but an amendment is part of the Constitution and so enters the clause as part of the first item, which is why a summary that lists them separately is describing the hierarchy rather than the words. State constitutions are the classic case the clause is aimed at, since it ends by saying that the judges in every state shall be bound by the federal instruments any thing in a state law to the contrary notwithstanding.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause requires of a law before it counts, and of a treaty before it counts.

questions.topic: The offices whose occupants the Senate must confirm
questions.learningObjective: list the diplomatic offices named in the appointment clause
questions.stem: The clause on appointment names several offices whose occupants may be appointed only with the advice and consent of the Senate. Which set of offices does that clause name?

options.text: Ambassadors appointed by the President with consent given by the Senate only after the appointment is made
options.misconception: moves the consent step to after the appointment is made

options.text: Ambassadors chosen by the Senate from among its own members for fixed terms of office
options.misconception: believes the Senate appoints ambassadors from its own members

options.text: Ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, together with the judges of the supreme Court
Ambassadors and consuls alone, since the clause makes no mention of public ministers
options.misconception: believes the clause makes no mention of public ministers

questions.explanation: The clause provides that the President shall nominate, and by and with the advice and consent of the Senate shall appoint, ambassadors, other public ministers and consuls, judges of the supreme Court, and all other officers of the United States whose appointments are not otherwise provided for and which shall be established by law. Public ministers sit between ambassadors and consuls in the list, and a summary that keeps ambassadors and consuls while dropping ministers has dropped a term the clause uses. The verb is nominate and appoint in sequence, so the consent is a step in the appointment rather than a review of a finished one, and the Senate appoints nothing itself: it consents, and the President then makes the appointment. The clause also lets Congress by law vest the appointment of inferior officers elsewhere, so the list is not closed in the way the first sentence suggests.
questions.hint: Read the list in the clause in order and notice which term a summary is likely to skip.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The life of a recess appointment
questions.learningObjective: state how long a commission granted during a Senate recess lasts
questions.stem: One clause lets the President fill a vacancy that arises while the Senate is not sitting. How long does the commission he grants in that recess last?

options.text: Until the Senate confirms a nominee, however many sessions that may take
options.misconception: assumes the appointment must wait for the Senate to act

options.text: Until the end of the Senate's next session after the recess in which the vacancy arose
For the remainder of the President's own term of office, whatever the Senate then does
options.misconception: ties the commission to the end of the presidential term

options.text: For one year from the day the commission is granted, and then it lapses
options.misconception: borrows a one-year rule that belongs to an army appropriation

questions.explanation: The words are that the President may fill up all vacancies that may happen during the recess of the Senate, by granting commissions which shall expire at the end of their next session. The two ends of the sentence therefore fit together: the recess is what creates the vacancy the clause reaches, and the Senate's next session is what ends the commission. The expiry is tied to the Senate's calendar rather than to the President's term, so a new administration does not inherit the earlier recess appointment, and it is not a fixed number of months either. And because the clause expires the commission, the appointee must be submitted to the Senate at the next session, which is what the appointment is for. The one-year figure belongs to a different subject, the limit on appropriations for the support of an army.
questions.hint: Ask what event ends the grant, and check whether the clause states a number of months or an event.

questions.topic: Measures that must be presented to the President
questions.learningObjective: identify which measures of a bicameral character reach the President
questions.stem: One clause extends the approval procedure for bills to measures that are not bills. Which measure must be presented to the President before it takes effect?

options.text: An order, resolution, or vote to which the concurrence of both houses is necessary, other than one on the question of adjournment
Any measure on which the two houses differ at all, including a concurrent resolution of the two chambers
options.misconception: sweeps in concurrent resolutions, which do not reach the President

options.text: A simple resolution of a single house, as soon as the other chamber has been told of it
options.misconception: believes a single-house resolution reaches the President

options.text: A joint resolution alone, and never an order or a vote to which both chambers have agreed
options.misconception: believes joint resolutions are the only covered measures

questions.explanation: The clause provides that every order, resolution, or vote to which the concurrence of the Senate and House of Representatives may be necessary, except on a question of adjournment, shall be presented to the President, and before the same takes effect shall be approved by him, or being disapproved by him shall be repassed by two thirds of the Senate and House, according to the rules and limitations prescribed in the case of a bill. The reach is set by a functional test, concurrence of both houses, and not by a label, so a joint resolution is covered but the test would reach other measures too, which rules out the fourth option as a rule. A one-house resolution is not a measure requiring concurrence of both, and the adjournment question is the single carve-out the clause itself makes.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause uses as its test for which measures are covered, and find the one exception it names.

questions.topic: The demand that puts yeas and nays in the journal
questions.learningObjective: compute the demand needed to record a vote in the journal
questions.stem: Ninety members of a chamber are present on a question. The clause that governs the journal requires a stated fraction of those present before the yeas and nays of the question must be entered on it. How many members must ask?

options.text: Twenty, because one fifth of a full chamber of one hundred seats is twenty
options.misconception: measures one fifth against the full hundred seats instead of those present

options.text: Thirty, because the same section sets expulsion at two thirds and half of two thirds is thirty
options.misconception: reuses the two-thirds figure that the same section sets for expulsion

options.text: Ninety, because a majority of those present is enough to require the record
options.misconception: raises the threshold from one fifth to a majority of those present

options.text: Eighteen, because the clause asks for the desire of one fifth of those present

questions.explanation: The clause provides that the yeas and nays of the members of either house on any question shall, at the desire of one fifth of those present, be entered on the journal. With ninety present, one fifth of ninety is eighteen, and eighteen members asking is enough. The denominator is those present, so fifteen is the wrong figure: it comes from one fifth of a full hundred seats, a chamber that is not full, and it understates the demand the clause sets. Thirty is borrowed from a different rule in the same section, which fixes expulsion at the concurrence of two thirds. And a majority is nowhere required; the clause deliberately sets a small threshold so that a small group can force a recorded vote on any question.
questions.hint: Divide the number present, not the number of seats, and check the fraction the clause names.

questions.learningObjective: identify the three powers listed together in one clause of Article I
questions.stem: One clause of Article I joins three powers in a single line. Which three are they?

options.text: To declare war, to grant letters of marque and reprisal, and to declare a blockade of an enemy's ports
options.misconception: adds a blockade power the clause does not name

options.text: To declare war, to provide for and maintain a navy, and to prescribe the rules of war
options.misconception: borrows words from the neighbouring navy and service clauses

options.text: To declare war, to grant letters of marque and reprisal, and to make rules concerning captures on land and water
To declare war, to make a treaty ending it, and to raise an army to fight it
options.misconception: substitutes the treaty power for the privateer and prize powers

questions.explanation: The clause gives Congress power to declare war, to grant letters of marque and reprisal, and to make rules concerning captures on land and water. The three are a package about war at sea, and a summary that swaps the second for a treaty or for maintaining a navy has moved the words in from neighbouring clauses. The fourth option fails the same way, since the authority to make rules for the government and regulation of the land and naval forces sits in its own clause, and that is a power over the services, not over the law of war. The third option adds a blockade, which the clause does not name, and that silence has its own separate history. Reading the clause as a whole shows that privateers and prize were understood as part of the war power itself, not as incidents of it.

questions.topic: How the authority to declare a blockade is accounted for
questions.learningObjective: explain the source of the blockade power that the war clause does not name
questions.stem: The clause covering war, privateers, and captures does not use the word blockade. How is the authority to declare one usually accounted for?

options.text: As a power the President may use only after the Senate concurs, because a blockade binds other nations
options.misconception: routes a blockade through the treaty clause

options.text: As a power implied in the power to declare war and to make rules concerning captures, a reading drawn from early practice
As a power expressly granted in the same clause, whose last line names the blockade in terms
options.misconception: believes the word blockade appears in the clause

options.text: As a power reserved to the several states until an act of Congress confirms the federal claim to it
options.misconception: treats a blockade as a power reserved to the states

The third option inverts the whole structure, since the war and prize powers are federal and the clause denies the states any treaty, alliance, or letters of marque at all. And a blockade was treated as an incident of the war power rather than as a compact with another nation, so it was not routed through the treaty clause, which is what the fourth option assumes.

questions.topic: The limit on appropriations for the support of an army
questions.learningObjective: state what the two-year limit in the armies clause attaches to
questions.stem: The clause that lets Congress raise and support armies carries a limit on appropriations. What is the limit, and what does it attach to?

options.text: No appropriation of money to that use may be for a term longer than two years
No army may be kept in the field for more than two years, whatever appropriations are made
options.misconception: reads the two-year term as a limit on the length of a conflict

options.text: No more than two years of appropriations for an army may be made in any single decade
options.misconception: invents a cumulative limit that the clause does not state

options.text: No appropriation for an army may run for more than one year, the limit used for a fleet
options.misconception: substitutes a one-year rule that does not exist

questions.explanation: The words of the clause are that no appropriation of money to that use shall be for a longer term than two years, and what the limit reaches is the term of the appropriation, not the length of a war. If a conflict outlasts the appropriation, Congress must appropriate again, which is a duty to renew rather than a power to end the conflict, and that distinction is the whole content of the second option's error. There is no cumulative figure anywhere in the clause, so the third option invents one. And the one-year limit belongs to no fleet provision in the Constitution at all; the neighbouring clause simply says that Congress may provide for and maintain a navy, so the fourth option substitutes a rule that does not exist.

questions.topic: Why the navy clause has no stated term

questions.learningObjective: state the two limbs of treason and the proof the Constitution requires

options.text: Levying war against the United States, or adhering to its enemies and giving them aid and comfort, proved by two witnesses to the same overt act or by a confession in open court
Levying war against the United States, or any breach of allegiance, proved by the testimony of a single witness
options.misconception: adds bare breach of allegiance and drops the two-witness rule

options.misconception: misnames who may be aided and narrows the proof rule

options.text: Levying war against the United States alone, with the second limb left to be created later by an act of Congress
options.misconception: believes the second limb was left to later legislation

questions.learningObjective: state the limits the Constitution places on the punishment of treason
questions.stem: One clause restricts the effects that may follow a conviction of treason. Which statement matches the restriction the clause imposes?

options.misconception: allows a post-mortem forfeiture the clause forbids

options.text: Congress may not declare a punishment for treason at all, which is left entirely to the courts in each case
options.misconception: denies the power to declare a punishment for treason

options.text: Congress may declare a punishment that works corruption of blood, which the clause merely discourages

The court held the provision unconstitutional, reasoning that a law must be presented to the President, and that the power to set aside what has been passed belongs to the President alone. The court described the defect as a bypass of the requirement that laws be presented to the President.

options.misconception: moves the summary into the treaty power and the consent to be given before

options.text: It allowed one chamber to undo legislation without the President's approval or disapproval of a bill

options.text: It allowed a chamber to refuse to appropriate money, which the summary treats as a defect
options.misconception: treats the power not to appropriate as the defect described

options.text: A state may not enter a treaty, alliance, or confederation, or an agreement or compact with a foreign power, or engage in war

questions.explanation: The tenth section of the first article forbids a state to enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation, and it forbids a state, without the consent of the national legislature, to enter into any agreement or compact with another state or with a foreign power, or to engage in war unless actually invaded or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay. The first option states both halves of the second prohibition, and the earlier part of the section separately denies the states the treaty power, which is the point of the word treaty in the first clause. The second and third options turn a prohibition into a reporting requirement, and the fourth tries to save an alliance by a distinction of words that the section does not make, since an alliance is one of the three things it names.
questions.hint: Read both sentences of the section and notice that the second one has a conditional exception of its own.

options.misconception: tries to buy permission with national money

options.text: A state may keep any force in peacetime, because the restriction applies only to war
options.misconception: reads a peacetime restriction as having no peacetime application

options.text: A state may not keep troops or ships of war in time of peace without the consent of the national legislature
A state may keep troops in peacetime but may not keep any ship of war at all
options.misconception: invents a peacetime bar on ships that the clause does not contain

questions.explanation: The clause provides that no state, without the consent of the national legislature, shall lay any duty of tonnage, keep troops, or ships of war in time of peace, or enter into any agreement or compact with another state or with a foreign power, or engage in war unless actually invaded or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay. The consent requirement, and not a flat prohibition, is what makes the first option right, and it explains why a state with an inherited coastal defence force was dealt with by legislation rather than by the clause alone. The second option invents a peacetime bar that the clause does not contain, the third tries to buy permission with money, and the fourth reads a restriction expressly limited to time of peace as if it had no application there at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the clause forbids the thing outright or makes it conditional on consent, and when it applies.

questions.learningObjective: state the exception that permits a state to act against a foreign power
questions.stem: A state is forbidden to engage in war without consent. What exception does the clause supply?

options.text: The state has notified the President of its intention to act at least thirty days in advance
options.misconception: substitutes advance notice for the condition of imminent danger

options.text: The state is actually invaded, or is in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay
The state has been requested to act by a foreign power that is itself under attack
options.misconception: treats a foreign request as one of the exceptions

options.text: The state legislature has voted to act by a two-thirds majority of both chambers
options.misconception: substitutes a legislative supermajority for necessity

questions.explanation: The clause ends with unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay, and the two conditions are alternatives. The first is a completed event of invasion and the second is a judgement about urgency that is deliberately narrow, since the point of the whole sentence is that a state may not use its own judgement to justify a war. The second option inverts the relationship, since a request from a foreign power is not among the exceptions and would make a state's war an instrument of another country's policy. The third substitutes a legislative supermajority that the clause does not mention, and the fourth substitutes a notice period for a condition of necessity, which is the opposite of what an imminent danger allows.
questions.hint: Find the words at the end of the sentence and ask whether the two conditions are alternatives.

questions.topic: An officer of the United States in Congress
questions.learningObjective: state the constitutional bar on officers serving in the legislature
questions.stem: One clause of Article I prevents a person from holding a federal office and a seat in Congress at the same time. What does it provide?

options.text: That no person holding any office under the United States may be a member of either house during the continuance of the office
That no person holding an office under the United States may vote in either house while the office lasts

options.misconception: extends the sentence to state offices it does not reach

options.text: That a person may hold a federal office provided the office was created by a statute rather than by the Constitution

questions.explanation: The clause provides that no person holding any office under the United States shall be a member of either house during his continuance in office, which is a bar on holding both at once and not a bar on voting or on a particular kind of office. That distinction is the whole of the difference between the first and second options, and the third option concerns state offices, which the sentence does not reach, though the neighbouring sentence in the same section does bar a member from an office created or increased in emoluments during his term. questions.explanation: The question is one of characterisation, and it has been framed by asking whether a payment to a foreign government is a loan within the meaning of the clause that bars spending without an appropriation, since a loan is money expected to be returned and is therefore a borrowing transaction. The influential early account treated a large wartime payment to an allied government as a payment rather than a loan, and traced the power to make it to the conduct of foreign affairs, and the line between the two categories has been argued ever since. The second option describes a sequencing question the appropriations clause raises, the third denies a consent requirement that the clause plainly states, and the fourth applies the uniformity condition of a different clause to a transaction that is not a tax.
questions.hint: Ask what makes a payment a loan, and which power a payment that is not a loan is traced to.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Where the two-thirds requirement sits in the treaty path
questions.learningObjective: locate the constitutional requirement in a diagram of the treaty process
questions.stem: A diagram of the treaty process has four nodes joined by three arrows. N1: the executive negotiates the terms of an agreement with another nation. N1 -> N2. N2: the agreement is laid before the Senate as a treaty. N2 -> N3. N3: a recorded vote is taken in the Senate. N3 -> N4. N4: the instrument is signed, the ratifications are exchanged, and the date the treaty itself provides for entry into force arrives. On which node does the requirement stated in the Constitution bear?

options.text: On N4, because the Constitution fixes the date on which a treaty enters into force
options.misconception: puts the requirement on the date of entry into force

options.text: On no node, because the Constitution lays down no requirement for treaties at all
options.misconception: denies that the clause states any requirement

options.text: On N3, because the Constitution fixes the fraction of the senators present that must concur
On N1, because the Constitution requires the terms to be negotiated by the executive
options.misconception: puts the requirement on the negotiation rather than the vote

questions.explanation: The Constitution fixes the requirement at the voting node. The clause provides that the President has power, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two thirds of the senators present concur, and the vote is the step at which that condition is satisfied or not, so the requirement bears on N3 and nowhere else in the diagram. N1 is where the negotiation happens, and the Constitution says who negotiates without imposing a condition there. N4 is the stage at which the treaty takes effect according to its own terms, and the date is a matter of the instrument rather than of the Constitution, which is the error in the third option. The fourth option is excluded because the clause is explicit.
questions.hint: Ask which step in the diagram is the step the clause actually prescribes, and what it prescribes there.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why the war power is written into the legislature's list
questions.learningObjective: explain the reasoning behind placing the war power in the legislature
questions.stem: Explain why the framers placed the power to declare war in the list of powers given to the legislature rather than to the President, and what follows for the President's authority while a war is under way.

answer.exemplar: The list of powers in the first section of the first article gives the legislature the power to declare war, to grant letters of marque and reprisal, to make rules concerning captures, to raise and support armies, to provide for and maintain a navy, to make rules for the government and regulation of the land and naval forces, and to provide for calling forth the militia. Several features of that arrangement point the same way. The power to declare war is placed beside the power to raise and support armies and to make rules for the forces, and those powers all depend on taxation and borrowing, which only the legislature can supply, so a declaration that could not be paid for would be empty. The clause that limits appropriations for the support of an army to a term of two years puts the legislature in a position where it must decide again whether a war continues, which is a decision about money rather than about fighting. Keeping the militia clauses in the same list matters too, because the President is Commander in Chief of the militia only when it is called into the actual service of the United States, and the calling is a legislative act. The consequence for the President is that the authority to conduct a war comes from the office itself once the war exists, and the disputes that follow are about the scope of that authority rather than about whether the office includes it. The Constitution does not define the extent of the command, which is why the framework used to analyse a claim divides the situations into those where the legislature has said nothing, those where it has authorised, and those where it has refused, and treats the last as the case in which the power is at its lowest ebb. A good answer should also notice what the text does not say: it does not fix a period within which the legislature must act, it does not say that the President's orders bind the legislature, and it does not mention any power to declare a blockade, which is why that authority is accounted for by inference from the war and prize powers rather than by quotation.

questions.explanation: A full answer has to connect the war clause to the neighbouring clauses that make it work, and then to say what that implies for the President's authority once a war exists. The powers to raise and support armies, to maintain a navy, and to make rules for the forces all sit in the same list and all depend on money the legislature alone supplies, and the two-year limit on appropriations for the support of an army forces a further decision as a war continues. Because the President is Commander in Chief of the militia only when it is called into the actual service of the United States, and the calling is legislative, even the domestic militia power is routed through the legislature in time of war. From those facts it follows that the authority to conduct a war is a power of the office once the war has been made, and that the live questions are about its extent and about what to do when the legislature disagrees. The text is silent on a period for legislative action, on any power to declare a blockade, and on any duty of the legislature to approve an ongoing campaign, so an answer that asserts any of those has gone beyond the text.
questions.hint: Start with the clauses that sit next to the war clause, then ask what the President's authority must rest on once a war exists.
